# Anamatagga Saṁyutta (SN 15)
**ID:** SN 15
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Anamatagga Saṁyutta
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/sn15
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0302m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Anamatagga Saṁyutta* (SN 15) is the fifteenth chapter of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, situated within the *Nidānavagga* [Bodhi 2003]. It comprises twenty discourses organized into two chapters (*vagga*s) [Hazra 1994; SuttaCentral]. Its unifying theme is the fathomless, unbounded temporal extent of rebirth (*saṁsāra*), countering mythological creation narratives by emphasizing that the ultimate beginning of existence cannot be discerned or known [Bodhi 2003; Nyanatiloka 1938; SuttaCentral]. The core homily repeated throughout the collection declares that for beings hindered by ignorance and bound by craving who roam and wander on, no prior limit (*pubbā koṭi*) is known [Shenghai Li 2012; Bodhi 2003]. The Buddha illustrates this vast duration through evocative similes, including mountains of bones left by a single person over eons, tears wept in grief, and maternal milk consumed across successive lifetimes [SuttaCentral].
The title term *anamatagga* has attracted extensive philological and doctrinal analysis. The commentary (*Sāratthappakāsinī*) resolves it as *anu-amatagga*, glossing that even if one pursues the beginning through knowledge (*ñāṇena anugantvā*) for centuries or millennia, it remains unthought-of and undiscoverable (*amatagga* / *aviditagga*) [Silk 2015; Bodhi 2003]. Its Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit counterpart is *anavarāgra* ("without lower or upper limit"), with cognates in Prakrit (e.g. Ardhamāgadhī *aņavadagga*) and Chinese translations rendering it as "without beginning" (*wushi*) or "without limit" [Silk 2015; Shenghai Li 2012]. In Theravāda historical chronicles, the *Anamatagga Saṁyutta* is remembered as the sermon delivered by the elder Rakkhita to convert the region of Vanavāsa after the Third Council [Gombrich et al. 1994; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. In northern scholasticism, the sutta's opening passage was frequently cited by Madhyamaka commentators—including Qingmu, the *Akutobhayā*, Buddhapālita, and Candrakīrti's *Prasannapadā*—to debate the reality versus emptiness of *saṁsāra* [Shenghai Li 2012].
Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral demonstrate close correspondences across the Chinese Āgamas, primarily in both translations of the *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99, SA 937–956; T 100, SA2 330–350) and four discourses of the *Ekottarāgama* (T 125, EA 51.1–2, 52.3–4), as well as EA2 30, SA3 11, and T 765.3 [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus confirms these relationships, identifying automatic cross-language alignments with the Chinese *Ekottarāgama*, the Tibetan translation of Śamathadeva's *Abhidharmakośaṭīkopayikā* (D4094), Madhyamaka treatises (*Akutobhayā*, D3829; Buddhapālita, D3842), the *Saṃghāṭasūtra*, the *Yogācārabhūmi*, and the *Sukhāvatīvyūha* [DharmaNexus]. Within Pali literature, DharmaNexus registers over 4,700 matching passages across 181 texts, including substantial shared material with other *Saṁyuttanikāya* collections (SN 22, SN 56, SN 35, SN 13, SN 14), several books of the *Aṅguttaranikāya* (AN 7, AN 5, AN 3), and the *Cullaniddesa* [DharmaNexus].
